1: The Voynich Manuscript, this 15th century book made of calfskin parchment, is dubbed the world's most mysterious book. It contains 240 pages of an untranslatable script that looks like a real language but doesn't match any known alphabet. Some pages are missing, too. The surreal illustrations found in the book are an enigma. Plants that don't exist, alien-like creatures, celestial charts with zodiac signs, naked women sitting in bathtub-like contraptions and what might be medieval alchemical equipment. Discovered in 1912 by rare book dealer Wilfred Voynich, the manuscript's history is clearer than its contents. It's believed to have belonged to Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II in the 16th century and a 17th century alchemist from Prague. But before that, no one really knows. It's been carbon dated to the early 1400s, yet no one has cracked its code. Theories about its purpose range from a secret cipher to a hoax and a health guide for medieval spy enthusiasts. Even modern cryptologists have tried and failed to decode it. Some theories link it to Hebrew or suggest it's a constructed language, but none hold up to scrutiny. So the manuscript stays a mystery sitting in Yale University's library. The Nazi Bell, die Glocke, or Project Kronos, was a supposed top-secret Nazi superweapon. Allegedly developed in the 1940s in Nazi Germany, it was a bell-shaped device about 12 feet high and 9 feet in diameter. Rumor has it it was some kind of anti-gravity machine for a flying saucer prototype and time travel experiment at the same time. Inside were two counter-rotating cylinders filled with a mysterious purple radioactive substance, possibly irradiated mercury, set to create plasma for propulsion or weapons. The testing site for this thing was a concrete structure in Poland dubbed Dehenge or the Fly Trap near the Wenceslaus Mine. Overseen by SS General Hans Kamla and powered by hydroelectricity, the project reportedly used concentration camp labor. By the war's end, all involved scientists were killed and the device was moved to an unknown location. Some say it traded to the US military for Kamla's freedom. Skeptics argue it's all a myth, dismissing the hench as a cooling tower for a power station. Polish author Igor Witkowski claimed the Glockus existence was revealed in declassified World War II documents, including a statement where SS General Jakob Sporenberg confessed to taking out 60 people tied to the project. Other high-ranking SS members were also implicated in the research. Some believe the bell now lies hidden in a Nazi gold train buried in Poland. The Black Stone, set in the eastern corner of the Kaaba in Mecca, is an Islamic relic revered for centuries. Before Islam, the Kaaba was already sacred, linked to pre-Islamic pilgrimage by the Nabateans. The history of the Black Stone is shrouded in mystery. Islamic tradition says Prophet Muhammad embedded the black stone into the Kaaba in 605 AD, but over time it shattered and was encased in a silver frame. One legend says it was placed into the original Kaaba by Adam. It was said to be dazzling white at first, but turned black due to the sins of those who touched it. After being lost during Noah's flood, the angel Jibreel revealed its location to Ibrahim, who embedded it into the Kaaba with the help of his son Ismael. Another legend imagines the Black Stone as a punished angel from the Garden of Eden. The angel failed to prevent Adam from eating the forbidden fruit and was turned into a jewel. It was said to have been placed on Mount Abu Kubais before Ibrahim brought it to the Kaaba Some believe it a meteorite while others speculate connections to Roman Emperor Ili Gabalus He brought a sacred black meteorite representing the sun god Ili Gabal from Syria to Rome. After his death, the stone was returned to Syria but later vanished. Some speculate it reappeared among Arab tribes and became the revered black stone of Islam. The Black Stone has faced numerous desecrations. During the Umayyad siege of Mecca in 683, it was shattered by a catapult. In the year 930, the Karmatians stole it and tried to reroute the Hajj to their base in Hajar, but failed. They returned it 23 years later after ransoming it for a hefty sum. In the 11th century, a man sent by the Fatimid Caliph tried to smash the stone, but caused only minor damage before being taken out. The ring or seal of Solomon is a legendary magical ring linked to the Israelite King Solomon. Often depicted as a pentagram or hexagram, the ring, made of brass and iron, supposedly gave Solomon dominion over demons, djinn and spirits, protection against evil and the ability to speak with animals and control the wind. According to legend, the ring was engraved by God and given to Solomon by the archangel Michael, with one half commanding good spirits and the other controlling evil ones. The ring bears an inscription believed to hold God's secret name, granting its wearer unparalleled power. One tale describes a demon stealing the ring and ruling in Solomon's place. Eventually, the demon threw the ring into the sea, where it was swallowed by a fish. A fisherman later caught the fish, unknowingly feeding it to Solomon, thus restoring his throne. No one knows where the ring is or if it ever existed. Some believe it was lost forever, hidden with Solomon's remains or kept secret by mystical orders. Others suggest it may resurface during the apocalypse. The Holy Grail The classic tale connects the Holy Grail to the cup Jesus used at the Last Supper and Joseph of Arimathea, who allegedly used it to catch Christ's blood during the crucifixion and preserve the grail afterwards. The grail first appears in a 12th century poem where it isn't even a cup, but more like a tray or bowl. The idea of Joseph of Arimathea and the grail's holy powers didn't emerge until tales from the 13th century. Some theories, like in the Da Vinci Code, suggests the Grail is a metaphor for a royal bloodline, implying Jesus had a family with Mary Magdalene. However, there's no evidence for this. Many have searched for the Grail in places like England, Scotland and France, but none have found it. Even the Nazis were rumored to have sought it during World War II. In Arthurian legends, the Grail is described as a cup, dish or stone with healing powers. It's guarded by the Fisher King, the last of a royal bloodline. Legends say it was brought to Britain by Joseph of Arimathea, hidden in a spring in Glastonbury. The rod of Moses, or staff of God, is mentioned in the Bible and Quran as a powerful object used by Moses for miraculous acts, such as parting the Red Sea and producing water from a rock. In the Bible, it is first introduced in Exodus, where Moses' staff is transformed into a snake and used in several miracles during the plagues of Egypt. It also plays a key role in the battle at Rephidim between the Israelites and the Amalekites. There is much speculation about what happened to Moses' staff. Some sources state that after the fall of Solomon's temple in 587 BC, it was passed down through generations. Others claim the staff was kept as a relic in Constantinople and later moved to France. Today it is said to be on display in the sacred relics collection at the Topkapi Palace in Istanbul Turkey having been brought there by Sultan Selim I after his conquest of Egypt in 1517 A Hadith collection from Shia Muslim tradition claims that Moses staff along with other prophetic relics, is preserved by them. The Shroud of Turin is a Christian relic believed by some to be the burial cloth of Jesus Christ. This ancient linen cloth, measuring about 14 feet long, bears the faint image of a man who appears to have suffered crucifixion, complete with wounds consistent with a crown of thorns and a spear to the side. The origins of the Shroud are steeped in mystery. It first appeared in historical records in the 14th century, but many believe it dates back much further. According to legend, the Shroud was secretly transported from Jerusalem to Edessa, then Constantinople, and finally to its current resting place in Turin, Italy. The Shroud's authenticity has been subject of intense debate. In 1988, carbon dating suggested it was a medieval creation, but critics argue that the sample tested may have been contaminated or from a repaired section. Other studies point to pollen and textile evidence linking it to 1st century Jerusalem. The Ark of Gabriel is a modern legend about a deadly artifact supposedly discovered beneath the Grand Mosque in Mecca. It's linked to Archangel Gabriel, sacred in both Christian and Islamic traditions. It's described in a manuscript titled Gabriel's Instructions to Muhammad, allegedly hidden by the Eastern Orthodox Church during the 1204 Crusader's sack of Constantinople. The document claims Gabriel entrusted the prophet Muhammad with a box of immense power, forbidden to be used until Resurrection Day and buried in the place of worship of angels before the creation of man, identified as Mecca. Legend says the Ark was hidden beneath the Grand Mosque. In 2015, construction work at the mosque supposedly unearthed it, triggering a catastrophic plasma emission. A crane collapse killed over 100 people on September 11th and a deadly stampede occurred weeks later, both connected to the attempts to move the Ark. Official explanations cited weather and overcrowding. After the incident, emissaries contacted Patriarch Kirill, believing the Church's possession of Gabriel's instructions to Muhammad could help safely manage the Ark. Two months later, the Pope and Patriarch Kirill met for the first time in nearly a thousand years, where it's speculated the Pope shared missing information from the Hagia Sophia manuscript. After the meeting, Patriarch Kirill traveled to Antarctica, reportedly to perform a ritual using the instructions. Around this time, President Putin ordered a mission to transport the Ark to Antarctica to the Holy Trinity Russian Orthodox Church. In December 2015, Russian warships docked in Jeddah near Mecca. Some say this is not the Ark of Gabriel, but the Ark of Satan or Lucifer. That's why it got taken to the fallen angels imprisoned in Antarctica. The whole story remains a mystery. The Ark of the Covenant or Ark of God is the most sacred relic of the Israelites. Described in the Hebrew Bible as a gold-covered chest, it is said to have housed the Ten Commandments. The Ark was believed to possess immense power, capable of parting rivers, toppling walls, and even serving as a divine weapon in battles. It was carried by priests during the Israelites' 40 years of wandering in the desert. Unauthorized handling of the Ark led to death. However, its whereabouts have been a mystery since its disappearance before the Babylonian siege of Jerusalem in 587 BC. One theory involves Prophet Jeremiah, who hid it in the Judean desert. He apparently stopped followers from marking the Ark's location, claiming it would remain hidden until God gathers his people and shows mercy. Despite this prophecy, illegal excavations around Mount Nebo persist, but the Jordanian government prosecutes such activities. Archaeologists have also explored Mount Sinai as a potential site with many associating it with Jebel Musa in Egypt though other possible sites across Saudi Arabia Yemen and Jordan are also considered Some speculate the Ark lies beneath the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, protected by vaults King Solomon allegedly built, but political and religious issues have stopped further exploration. More claims suggest that the Knights Templar brought it to Europe during the Crusades, or that it is hidden in Antarctica, tied to bizarre Nazi expeditions. Archaeological digs in the Judean desert, including the discovery of the dead sea scrolls, fuel hopes that the Ark might still be hidden there, in undiscovered caves. Meanwhile, in Aksum, Ethiopia, the Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion houses what locals claim is the Ark, guarded by monks who purportedly suffer early deaths. The Holy Lands, also called the Spare of Lungeness or Spare of Destiny, is believed to be the weapon that pierced Jesus' side during his crucifixion, though it's only briefly mentioned in the Christian Bible. By the 6th century, relics claiming to be parts of the Holy Lands began to appear, with the earliest known reference found in Jerusalem. Through the centuries, these relics traveled across Europe. Some were lost in the chaos of invasions, like when Alaric and his Visigoths allegedly stole it during the sack of Rome in 410. Others, like the version later found in Constantinople, were carried by crusaders and later by figures like Saint-Louis, who brought it to Paris in the 13th century. However, the relic would soon disappear after the French Revolution. In 1938, Adolf Hitler became obsessed with it, believing it would grant him ultimate power. After invading Austria, he seized what he thought was the spare of destiny, but by the end of World War II, it vanished into a hidden vault. Allied forces recovered it and gave it back to the Austrians, but its authenticity remained a subject of dispute. Today, the version of the lands displayed in Vienna in the Imperial Treasury has the most documented history, dating back to Charlemagne, who reportedly carried it during many victorious campaigns. But its true origins continue to spark mystery and debate, with some claiming the lands is hidden in the Vatican archives or disputing its existence. The Sintamani stone is a mystical, wish-fulfilling jewel rooted in Hindu and Mahayana Buddhist traditions, often likened to the philosopher's stone. Described as a luminous pearl, it's said to manifest desires, cure diseases and grant divine wisdom. In Hinduism, the stone is associated with Vishnu and Ganesha, sometimes depicted on the forehead of the Naga king Mani or the legendary sea creature Makara. In Buddhism, it's held by divine beings and is often seen atop the wind horse on Tibetan prayer flags. Reciting its small hymn is believed to grant Buddha-like wisdom. The stone is also tied to Tibetan myths, said to have arrived in a chest from the heavens and powers the mythical Himalayan kingdom of Shambhala. Its influence even extends to Japan, where the goddess Lakshmi is often depicted holding it. The Balinese Kintamani region is named after this legendary relic. The Imperial Seal of China was crafted from the sacred Heshibi Jade in 221 BC. It symbolized the Mandate of Heaven, an ancient Chinese political ideology that legitimized the ruler's power. It was created by Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of China, after uniting the country under the Qin dynasty. The seal made from jade symbolized immortality and inner beauty in Chinese culture. Jade was so closely associated with immortality that some people attempted to drink it in liquid form to gain eternal life. As the seal passed through various dynasties, it became a key symbol of legitimacy, and whoever held it was seen as the rightful ruler. However, after dynasties rose and fell, the seal was lost by the 10th century, but it was never recovered.

1: The pentagram is a five-pointed star that already appeared on Sumerian pottery around 3500 BC, where it was linked to powerful deities such as Ishtar or Marduk. Pentagrams dating back about 5,000 years have also been found in China's Liangzhu culture. In ancient Greece, the symbol was known by at least the 6th century BC and used by Pythagoreans as a sign of mutual recognition, well-being, good deeds and charity. During the Middle Ages in Christendom, the upright pentagram represented the five senses and the five holy wounds of Christ. Within later witchcraft traditions, it represented the balance of the five elements. In modern pagan and Wiccan use, an upright, often encircled pentagram known as a pentacle is seen as a symbol of protection. However, if inverted, the meaning changes. The upside-down pentagram became associated with Lucifer, – Satanism, black ritual, magic and the summoning of demons. This interpretation was strongly popularized by occultist Elipha Levi and later adopted by the Church of Satan. During the 20th century satanic panic, pentagrams were widely censored and their appearance as graffiti was often wrongly treated as evidence of organized criminal cults. In the late 1990s, some US schools attempted to ban students from wearing pentagrams on clothing or jewelry due to fear of the occult. Signal bands have also been common in religious schools and workplaces, particularly in Christian settings. The symbol has also been removed from Magic the Gathering cards and video games like Diablo 3 or World of Warcraft due to parental complaints. The Hooked Cross or Hakenkreuz is a specific variation of the swastika that became the official symbol of National Socialist Germany in 1920. The symbol appeared on flags, armbands, uniforms, badges and medals. Adolf Hitler personally selected the final design, a black right-facing 45-degree swastika set in a white circle on a red background. Red represented the social idea of the movement, distinct from Marxist socialism. White represented nationalism, and the swastika symbolized the Aryan race and productive labor. The colors also echoed the imperial German flag. Due to its connection to the Nazi regime, the Hooked Cross is still legally restricted or banned in Germany, Austria, France, Poland, Russia, Ukraine, Australia, Brazil and others under hate speech or extremism laws. These laws specifically target the Nazi-hooked cross and not the ancient religious swastika used in Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism. Some communist symbols are seen as very controversial. The hammer and sickle represents unity between industrial workers and agricultural peasants. It was first adopted during the Russian Revolution and became the symbol for the Soviet Union. The red five-pointed star symbolizes the spread of communism across the five inhabited continents. It became a key military emblem for the Bolsheviks and the Red Army. The plain red flag represents socialism, communism, anarchism, and the broader labor movement and is often displayed alongside other communist symbols. These symbols, including the USSR flag in particular, are banned or restricted in the Czech Republic, Austria, Georgia, Indonesia, Latvia, Poland, Lithuania, South Korea, where variants linked to North Korea are also restricted, and Ukraine. The bans are rooted in the historical trauma of former Soviet states, where these symbols are associated with repression, forced collectivization, mass famines and genocide. Some governments also cite their continued use by modern far-left terrorist groups like the Shining Path in Peru and the Naxalite insurgents in India. The Schutzstaffel insignia includes several distinct symbols related to the paramilitary organization of the Nazi Party. The SS runes or Doppelsieg rune were the primary emblem on uniforms flags or banners and were so widely used that German typewriters during the Nazi era added a dedicated key for it The Death's Head was associated with the SS Totenkopfverbände unit overseeing concentration camps. The Wolfsangel, an ancient heraldic symbol, was used by Waffen-SS divisions like Das Reich and Landsturm Nederland. The Odal rune, historically representing heritage or inheritance, was stylized with wings or feet by the SS to symbolize kinship, blood ties and Aryan purity, notably used by the SS Race and Settlement Main Office and the 7th Mountain Division Prinz Eugen. In 2021, the Odal rune drew attention when a stage shape at CPAC in Florida resembled its form, sparking controversy. Many of these symbols are adopted today by neo-Nazis and white supremacists as a way to display Nazi affiliation while avoiding the more recognizable Hakenkreuz. Like other Nazi symbols, most SS insignia are banned in their stylized forms in numerous countries like Germany, Austria, Poland, Russia, France, Hungary, the Czech Republic and Ukraine, where public display, distribution and production are prohibited and sentenced with up to three years in prison. The Z symbol is one of several markings painted on Russian military vehicles involved in the Ukraine war. It's believed to help distinguish units and prevent friendly fire, but the exact meaning remains unclear. The symbol has become a militarist emblem in Russian propaganda and is used by civilians to show support for the war. The Czech Republic classifies it as equivalent to the Hakenkreuz. It's also banned in Estonia, Georgia, Germany, where displaying it is a felony punishable by up to three years in prison, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Moldova and of course Ukraine. The Confederate battle flag, showing a blue St. Andrew's cross with white stars on a red field, was created for battlefield identification during the American Civil War. Although it was never the official flag of the Confederacy, it became its most recognized symbol. The flag was revived during the Civil Rights era, where it was used as a sign of resistance to desegregation and racial equality. Supporters describe it as a symbol of Southern heritage and pride. Critics link it to white supremacy and racism. The flag has been increasingly restricted or removed from public use in the United States. It's banned from military bases and Department of Defense installations, including US Navy and Marine contexts. Mississippi replaced its state flag in 2020 to eliminate the Confederate emblem, and New York banned its display or sale on state property. Retailers such as Walmart removed the flag from sale, NASCAR banned it from events, and private sites like Hollywood Cemetery in Richmond, Virginia prohibited its display. In Ireland, the Cork Gaelic Athletic Association banned the flag from matches due to its association with racism. In Germany, if used by neo-Nazis or extremist groups to promote hate or racism, it can be prosecuted. The Rising Sun Flag was used by Japan's military from 1870 until the end of World War II, symbolizing the sun goddess Amaterasu and Japan as the land of the Rising Sun. Its origins trace back to the Edo period, when feudal warlords used it. Today, the Japanese maritime and ground self-defense forces continue to use the flag, but it's controversial and restricted in countries like South and North Korea, Singapore, Malaysia, the Philippines, Taiwan and Australia due to its association with Japanese militarism and wartime atrocities. China has compared it to the Nazi swastika. The flag is banned by FIFA in international competitions, though Japan maintains that it is a traditional cultural symbol. The Blood Drop Cross or the mystic insignia of a clansman has been the most recognized symbol of the Ku Klux Klan since the early 1900s For clan members it represents the blood of Jesus Christ signifying a sacrifice for the white race and the purity of its blood. The symbol is closely tied to white supremacist ideology and has been used on robes, flags, literature and other materials to convey racial superiority and intimidation. In the US, it's generally legal to display but is widely recognized as a hate symbol and often censored in content moderation or media. Social media platforms like Nextdoor are listed as prohibited. New York state law banned its sale or display in public spaces and European football organizations like FARE monitor and limit its use in stadiums. In Germany it's banned as a hate symbol. The Celtic Cross originated in Ireland and Britain between the 9th and 12th centuries as part of Celtic Christianity. Its ringed design is said to have blended Christian symbolism with earlier pagan elements, such as the sun, helping ease the conversion of local populations. Traditionally, it has been widely used as a symbol of Irish heritage, faith, and Christian identity. In modern times, the symbol has become controversial due to the adoption of a specific stylized version by white supremacist groups. This version is typically shown as a simplified Black Cross within a circle and has been used by neo-Nazis and the Ku Klux Klan as a substitute for the Nazi swastika, especially in countries that banned it. This stylized version of the Celtic Cross is legally restricted or banned in Germany, Austria, Poland, Brazil, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Russia and Ukraine. The traditional Celtic High Cross used in religious and cultural settings is not banned. However, due to the extremist appropriation of the stylized version, the symbol is sometimes misinterpreted in public spaces and monitored by law enforcement and flagged by social media platforms as a hate emblem in specific contexts. The Black Sun, also known as the Sonnenrad or a form of sunwheel draws visual inspiration from much older symbols. Disc-like ornaments called zierscheiben, dating to the late Bronze Age around 800 BC, have been found in Alemanic and Frankish graves. The original meaning of these ancient sunwheels is unclear, and they are distinct from the Black Sun symbol later associated with Nazism. The Black Sun, as it is known today, is a 20th century Nazi reinvention. A specific version was installed in the 1930s at Wewelsburg Castle by Heinrich Himmler. The symbol was embedded in the floor of the Hall of Supreme SS Leaders and consists of 12 radial SIG runes, visually combining elements of the Sunwheel, the Swastika and the SS Victory Rune. This design appeared nowhere else in Nazi Germany and it's unknown whether it had an official name or defined meaning within the SS. The floor symbol remains in place today partially covered by furniture. In the 1990s, the symbol was revived by neo-Nazi groups and is now widely used. Because of its strong association with Nazism, the Black Sun is banned or restricted in many countries and monitored as a hate symbol. The ISIS Black Flag is used by Islamist extremist groups as a symbol of violent jihadism, presenting armed struggle as a means to establish an Islamic system of governance. It typically shows a black background with the Shahada, the Islamic declaration of faith, written in white Arabic calligraphy. The design draws from the black standards used during the Abbasid Revolution, when the black flag symbolized rebellion against the Umayyad Caliphate. The modern version was adopted and popularized by ISIS after its 2014 declaration of a caliphate. Since then, the flag has become one of the most controversial and heavily censored symbols in in global counter efforts It subject to legal bans criminal penalties and widespread removal on social media and digital platforms Due to its association with ISIS and related extremist groups variants of the flag are banned or restricted in countries including the United Kingdom, Australia, China, the Netherlands, Austria, Germany and others. Bans target the ISIS-specific variant, not all Shahada flags. The Ustasche emblem is a stylized blue capital U containing a grenade and served as the emblem of the Croatian fascist Ustasche movement during World War II. The group ruled the Nazi-aligned independent state of Croatia under Ante Pavelic. The symbol is directly linked to the regime's atrocities, including the killing of over 300,000 Serbs, Jews and Roma, and remains a source of ethnic tension in the Balkans. Austria outlawed the U-symbol and the NDH flag, with penalties including fines and possible imprisonment. In Germany, displaying Ustasche symbols is also illegal. In Croatia and Serbia, public display is restricted. The Circle A or Anarchist A is the primary symbol of the anarchist movement. It first appeared in the early 1960s, promoted by the Paris Libertarian Youth Group. The symbol spread via punk rock culture in the 1970s, representing the anarchist principle that society can function without hierarchical authority, summarized as anarchy is order. It evolved into variations including the punk version, where the A extends beyond the circle. While there are no formal bans, many institutions such as schools, prisons, and public spaces restrict its display due to associations with anti-establishment activity, civil disobedience, disorder, and radical leftist groups like Antifa. It's explicitly listed in US domestic terrorism guides as an anarchist violent extremism symbol. Common measures include graffiti removal and confiscation of protest gear. In 2018, Hamilton Canada officials classified the symbol as hate material and ordered its removal from a window, comparing it to the Nazi swastika. The Guy Fawkes mask is a stylized depiction of Guy Fawkes, a member of the Gunpowder Plot of 1605, an attempt to blow up the House of Lords in London. The mask gained recognition after the film adaptation of the graphic novel V for Vendetta. It was later adopted by the online hacktivist group Anonymous, representing digital rebellion, information freedom and opposition to government surveillance and corporate control. Anonymous has used the mask in cyber campaigns, targeting governments, corporations and organizations they view as corrupt or oppressive, like the Church of Scientology and authoritarian regimes. However, several Middle Eastern countries have banned the import and sale of the mask, triggered by Arab Spring protests where the mask was widely used. Nations such as Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and the UAE cite concerns over public safety and claim that the mask encourages violence and extremism. Falun Gong is a spiritual movement founded in China in the early 90s. Its primary emblem, the Falun or Law Wheel, represents a miniature form of the universe. The symbol features one large central swastika surrounded by four smaller counter-clockwise ones representing the Buddha school along with four Tai Chi symbols from Taoist tradition symbolizing the balance of masculine and feminine energies. However, since 1999 Falun Gong has been banned and heavily suppressed in mainland China, where the government labels it a subversive evil cult and sees it as a threat to social stability. Public display of the Falun Gong symbol is illegal and practitioners have faced mass arrests and persecution. In Russia, regional courts have banned Falun Gong literature as extremist, while in Indonesia practitioners are denied legal recognition and permanent residency due to pressure from China. Thank you.

Set in the Texas-Mexico borderlands of the 1850s, it follows a 14-year-old runaway, known as the Kid, who joins the real-life Galanton Gang, a group of hunters paid for Native American sculpts.
